reasons: x keeps all parsing in parser.go, as the package already did: parseFunctionCallExpr and parseTupleConsExpr sit beside parseObjectConsExpr and share parseExpressionList. y moves parseFunctionCallExpr into function_call_expr.go and parseTupleConsExpr into tuple_cons_expr.go, so parsing is split across files, and each copy repeats the same argument loop.

x names the new files ast_function_call_expr.go and ast_tuple_cons_expr.go, which matches ast_object_cons_expr.go and the other AST files. y's function_call_expr.go and tuple_cons_expr.go break that pattern, so the file names no longer show where the AST types live.

In x, each AST type reports its own traversals through a variables() method (on ObjectConsExpr, ObjectConsKeyExpr, FunctionCallExpr and TupleConsExpr). y instead puts a generic tree walk in Expression.Variables, so it depends on how the other types are built inside.

y's object-construct layout code is spread out: ObjectConsItem.init takes the separator tokens that come before the item, and splitAtLineEnd is a method on ObjectConsExpr that never uses its receiver. x keeps the layout decision in one free function, splitObjectTail, and keeps ObjectConsItem.init about the key and value only.

x's tests follow its file split: ast_function_call_expr_test.go covers function calls and tuples, including their Variables and round trip. y spreads the same feature over ast_expression_test.go, function_call_expr_test.go and parser_test.go.

y names its new files ast_function_call_expr.go and ast_tuple_cons_expr.go, which matches the package's existing ast_<type>.go pattern. x names them function_call_expr.go and tuple_cons_expr.go, so they sit apart from the other AST type files.

y keeps parseFunctionCallExpr and parseTupleConsExpr in parser.go next to parseObjectConsExpr, so all token partitioning stays in one place. x puts these parse functions inside the type files, splitting the parser across files, and the type files then call back into parser.go.
y adds a shared parseExpressionList in parser.go for the argument and element loops that the call and tuple parsers have in common. x writes the same partitioning loop twice, once in each new file.

In y, each composite type collects its own variables through a variables() method (ObjectConsExpr, ObjectConsKeyExpr, FunctionCallExpr, TupleConsExpr), so each type owns its part of Expression.Variables. One drawback: the shared expressionsVariables helper lives in ast_function_call_expr.go even though TupleConsExpr also uses it.

y's attach tracking (setAttached hooks spread across the node.go list methods) is more invasive than x's single parent pointer set in newNode. This is a smaller structural cost than x's misplaced parsers and file split.

x/ast_expression.go: Expression.Variables walks child nodes generically, so FunctionCallExpr and TupleConsExpr need no code for collecting variables. y/ast_expression.go makes Expression check for each wrapped type in turn and call a variables() method that it adds to ObjectConsExpr, FunctionCallExpr and TupleConsExpr. That ties Expression to every new type.

x/ast_object_cons_expr.go splits adding an item into focused helpers (isMultiline, takeTail, splitTail, splitAtLineEnd) and moves building the item into ObjectConsItem.init. y/ast_object_cons_expr.go puts multi-line detection, gap splitting, rebuilding the children and building the key all in one long appendItem. It also hangs receiver-free helpers (hasComma, newlineToken) on ObjectConsExpr.

x/function_call_expr.go and x/tuple_cons_expr.go keep the existing newXxx constructor pattern (like newObjectConsExpr). y builds these structs inline inside parseFunctionCallExpr and parseTupleConsExpr, which departs from the structure the package already had.

x/node.go adds one hook (setParent in newNode) and reuses the existing inTree.parent field. y/node.go adds a second field, holder, next to parent, and spreads setContentHolder calls across Detach, ReplaceWith, Clear, AppendNode and InsertNode, so tracking whether a node is attached is scattered through the list code.

y does have tidier test files: tuple_cons_expr_test.go mirrors its source file, and the parse tests stay in TestParse. x puts the tuple and call checks in ast_expression_test.go and parser_test.go. This is a smaller point than the source-file structure above.

y/node.go keeps the existing `inTree.parent` field and sets it in `newNode`. x/node.go adds a second field, `holder`, plus `setContentHolder` calls in Detach, ReplaceWith, Clear, AppendNode and InsertNode. That gives x two parent concepts doing the same job.

y's `Expression.Variables` walks child nodes through the existing `walkChildNodes`, so the new FunctionCallExpr and TupleConsExpr fit in without extra code. x needs a `variables()` method on ObjectConsExpr, FunctionCallExpr and TupleConsExpr, and `Expression.Variables` has to check each one with `As*` calls. Every new expression type must be added there by hand.

In y/ast_object_cons_expr.go, appending an item is split into helpers with one job each: `isMultiline`, `takeTail`, `splitTail`, `splitAtLineEnd`, `ObjectConsItem.init` and `separatorTokens`. Building a new item belongs to ObjectConsItem. x's `appendItem` is one method of about 100 lines that splits gaps, rebuilds children, places the tail and builds the key all at once.

y adds `newFunctionCallExpr` and `newTupleConsExpr` constructors, as the package already does with `newObjectConsExpr` and `newTraversal`. x/function_call_expr.go and x/tuple_cons_expr.go build these structs inline inside the parse functions.
x does have a small advantage in tests: each new source file has its own test file, such as x/tuple_cons_expr_test.go. y spreads these tests across ast_expression_test.go and parser_test.go.

x names the new files ast_function_call_expr.go and ast_tuple_cons_expr.go, which matches the existing ast_object_cons_expr.go. It keeps parseFunctionCallExpr and parseTupleConsExpr in parser.go next to parseObjectConsExpr. y adds function_call_expr.go and tuple_cons_expr.go without the ast_ prefix and puts the parse functions inside them, while parseObjectConsExpr stays in parser.go, so parsing is now split two different ways.

x writes the code shared by the two new types once: parseExpressionList in parser.go and expressionsVariables in ast_function_call_expr.go. y copies the same partition-and-append loop into both parse functions and the same variables loop into both types.

x's Expression.Variables (ast_expression.go) asks the wrapped node for a small variables() interface, so Expression does not need to know each wrapped type. y's version checks ObjectConsExpr, FunctionCallExpr and TupleConsExpr one by one, so every new wrapped type means another edit to Expression.

x splits ObjectConsExpr.appendItem into parts with one job each: isMultiline, splitObjectTail, ObjectConsItem.init and newObjectConsKeyExprFor. y's appendItem is about 100 lines that work out the layout, rebuild the children list and build the key in one method. It also adds isLineEnd, hasComma and newlineToken as ObjectConsExpr methods that never use the receiver.
In node.go, x adds a single attached flag and one setAttached helper. y adds a holder pointer next to the old parent field, so inTree now has two overlapping ways to record that a node is attached.

y keeps the new parse functions in parser.go next to parseObjectConsExpr: parseFunctionCallExpr, parseTupleConsExpr and the shared parseExpressionList all live there. x puts parseFunctionCallExpr and parseTupleConsExpr in function_call_expr.go and tuple_cons_expr.go. That breaks the existing split where parser.go builds the tree and the ast_*.go files hold the node types.

y names its new files ast_function_call_expr.go and ast_tuple_cons_expr.go, which matches ast_object_cons_expr.go and ast_expression.go. x's function_call_expr.go and tuple_cons_expr.go drop the ast_ prefix, so the AST types are split across two naming schemes.

In y, ObjectConsExpr.appendItem is broken into pieces that each do one job: ObjectConsItem.init, which mirrors Attribute.init; newObjectConsKeyExprFor; splitObjectTail; and isMultiline. x does all of this in one large appendItem, including building the key and the item. It also adds receiver methods (isLineEnd, hasComma, newlineToken) that never use the receiver.

y's Expression.Variables calls a small variables() interface on whatever expression it wraps, and ObjectConsKeyExpr.variables handles keys. Each node type owns its own variable collection. x's Expression.Variables checks each concrete type in turn, and ObjectConsExpr.variables reaches into the key's private literal flag.

Minor points against y: the shared helper expressionsVariables sits in ast_function_call_expr.go even though the tuple code uses it too, and the tuple tests live in ast_function_call_expr_test.go. x keeps the tests for each type in a separate file, which is tidier.
